blocks.text: These questions describe a study and ask what it actually proves. The whole skill rests on one insight: **“random” appears in study design twice, doing two completely different jobs**—and each job earns a different kind of conclusion.

rows: participants drawn at random **from a population**
the right to **generalize** results to that population
participants split at random **into treatment groups**
the right to conclude **cause and effect**

items: **Classify the study first:** did researchers *assign* treatments (experiment), or just observe and measure (observational study)?
**Match the verbs to the design:** observational → “is associated with”; randomized experiment → “likely causes.”
**Check both randoms separately.** Random selection without assignment generalizes but can't prove cause; random assignment of volunteers proves cause but only for people like the participants.
**Hunt the confounder** in observational claims: what third factor could drive both variables?
**Pick the strongest conclusion the design supports—and no stronger.** Overreach and underreach are both wrong.

blocks.text: Two-question checklist for every study: **Who got sampled, and how? Who got assigned, and how?** The answers dictate the conclusion almost mechanically.
Researchers **measure what's already happening**—no one is told what to do. *Survey adults about their coffee habits and their sleep.*
Researchers **randomly assign** participants to treatments. *Assign half to regular coffee, half to decaf; compare sleep.*
Can show: {teal|cause and effect}—if assignment was random.

Suppose heavy coffee drinkers in a survey sleep worse. Did coffee cause it? Maybe—or maybe people with **stressful jobs** both drink more coffee *and* sleep worse. That lurking third factor is a {rose|confounding variable}, and observation alone can never rule it out. Random assignment can: splitting people into groups by coin flip spreads the stressful jobs (and every other hidden factor) evenly across both groups, leaving the treatment as the only systematic difference.

blocks.stem: Researchers survey $500$ randomly selected adults about how often they exercise and how they rate their mood. Which best describes this study?
choices: An observational study, because no treatment was assigned to participants
An experiment, because the participants were selected at random
An experiment, because the sample size is large
Neither, because mood cannot be measured

items.text: Everyone kept their own habits; researchers only measured. Observation—despite the random sampling.
The trap this page exists for: random **selection** is about who gets surveyed. An experiment requires random **assignment** to treatments.
Size changes precision, never study type.
Self-reported ratings are measured in studies constantly—measurability isn't the issue.

blocks.text: “Randomly selected” does **not** make a study an experiment. Ask what happened *after* selection: assigned to groups, or just observed?

pages.title: What Conclusions Does a Design Support?

blocks.text: Cross the two ingredients and every study lands in one of four boxes:

rows: **cause**, but only for the participants (and people like them)
blocks.caption: Assignment controls the *cause* column; selection controls how far the result travels.

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Causation requires **random assignment**. Generalization requires **random selection**. Each “random” buys exactly one, never both.

Researchers recruit $2{,}000$ **volunteers** with insomnia and randomly assign half to a new sleep program and half to a waiting list. After eight weeks, the program group sleeps $45$ minutes longer per night on average. What's supported?

items.text: The program **likely caused** the sleep improvement among the participants.
items.note: Random assignment ✓ — comparable groups make the program the credible explanation.

items.text: The program will improve sleep for **all adults with insomnia**.
items.note: The participants were volunteers, not a random sample of that population—the causal result stays with people like them.

blocks.stem: A botanist randomly selects $400$ tomato plants from the thousands in a greenhouse, then randomly assigns half to receive Fertilizer X and half to receive no fertilizer. After a month, the Fertilizer X plants are substantially taller on average. Which is the best conclusion?
choices: Fertilizer X is likely the cause of the greater growth for plants in this greenhouse
Fertilizer X is associated with greater growth, but no causal conclusion can be drawn
Fertilizer X will cause greater growth for all tomato plants everywhere
No conclusion can be drawn, because plants respond differently to fertilizer

items.text: Both randoms present: assignment earns **cause**, selection earns generalization to **this greenhouse's** plants. The strongest supported claim—and not a syllable stronger.
Underreach: with random assignment, “association only” throws away exactly what the design paid for.
Overreach: the sample came from one greenhouse—“everywhere” was never sampled.
Variation between individual plants is why the study compares *group averages*—it doesn't void the conclusion.

blocks.text: The right answer is usually the **Goldilocks** choice: one option too strong, one too weak, one derailing—and one that claims precisely what the two randoms bought.
When a claim outruns its study, the SAT asks *why it isn't justified*. The usual suspects:

rows: the sample represents no one but itself
improvement can't be attributed—maybe everyone improves
a third factor tied to both variables
the causal story has a rival explanation
sampled one group, concluded about a bigger one
precision — the margin of error balloons

blocks.stem: A vitamin company emails a survey to its customers; $90$ reply, and $62\%$ of them report feeling healthier since starting the vitamin. The company claims its vitamin improves health for adults. Which statement best explains why the claim is **not** justified?
choices: The sample was not randomly selected from the population of adults, so the results may not represent adults in general
The sample size of 90 is too small for any statistical conclusion
The percentage 62% is too close to one-half to mean anything
The survey should have been conducted by phone rather than by email

items.text: Two layers of bias: only *customers* were emailed, and only the *willing* replied. No random selection → no reach beyond respondents—and with no comparison group, even “feeling healthier” has no benchmark.
Size is the lesser problem: $90$ randomly selected adults could support a (wide) estimate. A **biased** sample of $90{,}000$ still couldn't.
$62\%$ is a perfectly usable statistic; the issue is *whose* $62\%$ it is.
Changing the medium changes nothing about who was invited or who chose to answer.

blocks.text: When flaws compete, **bias beats size**. The SAT's favorite wrong answer blames the sample size when the real problem is that the sample was never random.
Run the checklist on each study—random selection? random assignment?—then find the conclusion that spends exactly what the design earned.

blocks.stem: A nutritionist randomly assigns each of $60$ participants to one of two breakfast plans and measures their reported energy levels after two weeks. Which best describes this study?
choices: An experiment, because participants were randomly assigned to treatments
An observational study, because energy levels were only reported
An experiment, because numerical data was collected
An observational study, because participants knew which plan they followed

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** The defining act of an experiment happened: the researcher **assigned** the treatments, at random.

items.text: Random assignment → comparable groups → the study can support causal comparisons of the plans.
How the outcome is measured (even self-reported) doesn't decide the type—assignment does.
Observational studies collect numbers too; data type is irrelevant to design.
Participants' awareness may matter for *blinding*, but the study is still an experiment.

blocks.stem: A study of $1{,}200$ randomly selected adults finds that those who nap at least three times per week report lower stress than those who don't nap. Which is the best conclusion?
choices: For adults, frequent napping is associated with lower reported stress
Frequent napping causes lower stress in adults
The association holds only for the 1,200 adults surveyed
No conclusion is possible without knowing why people nap

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** Random selection ✓, random assignment ✗ → an **association** that **generalizes** to adults. Exactly that, no more, no less.

items.text: The Goldilocks conclusion for the top-right box of the grid.
Nobody was assigned to nap—confounders (flexible schedules, less demanding jobs) could drive both variables. No causation.
Underreach: random selection is precisely the license to extend the association to the adult population.
Unknown motives block *causal* claims, not associational ones—the pattern itself is a finding.

blocks.stem: Researchers recruit adult **volunteers** who experience frequent headaches and randomly assign each to receive either a new medication or a placebo. The medication group reports significantly fewer headaches. Which is the best conclusion?
choices: The medication likely caused the reduction in headaches for participants, and for people similar to them
The medication will reduce headaches for all adults
The medication is associated with fewer headaches, but causation cannot be concluded
The placebo group's results should be discarded

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** Random assignment ✓ earns causation; volunteer recruitment ✗ limits the reach to the participants and people like them—the bottom-left box of the grid.

items.text: Cause: yes. Reach: limited. Both randoms accounted for.
“All adults” needs random selection from all adults—volunteers with headaches aren't that.
Underreach: with random assignment and a placebo control, causal language is exactly what the design supports.
The placebo group is the **comparison** that makes the result meaningful—discarding it would destroy the study.

blocks.stem: A principal notices that students who chose to use a study app have higher grades than students who didn't, and wants to determine whether the app **causes** higher grades. Which change to the study design would best support such a conclusion?
choices: Randomly assign students to use the app or not, then compare grades
Survey a larger number of students who already use the app
Ask the app's users how satisfied they are with it
Compare the app users' grades with those of last year's students

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** The current design is observational with self-selection—motivated students may both choose the app *and* earn higher grades. Random assignment spreads motivation (and every other hidden factor) evenly, isolating the app's effect.

items.text: Random assignment is the only listed change that removes the confounding—the coin flip, not the student, decides.
More of a self-selected group is more of the same bias—size never fixes selection.
Satisfaction measures opinion of the app, not its effect on grades.
Last year's students differ in courses, teachers, and cohort—swapping one non-comparable group for another.

blocks.title: Things to Remember
items: Two randoms, two jobs: {blue|random selection} → **generalize** to the population; {teal|random assignment} → **cause and effect**. Each buys one, never both.
Experiment = researchers assign treatments; observational study = researchers only measure. Random *selection* alone does not make an experiment.
Observational findings are **associations**—a confounding third variable can always be driving both sides.
Volunteers cap the reach: causal results from assigned volunteers apply to the participants and people like them.
Flawed-claim questions: **bias beats size**—look for self-selection, missing control groups, and population overreach before blaming sample size.
Choose the Goldilocks conclusion: everything the design earned, and nothing it didn't.
